claims.text: Marienplatz is the central square of Munich's inner city and has been the city's main square since its founding in 1158 by Henry the Lion.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The square was originally called Markth (market), Schranne, and later Schrannenplatz (grain market square).
claims.subject: self

claims.text: In 1315, Emperor Ludwig the Bavarian granted Munich market freedom with the condition that the square remain unbuilt for all time.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: During the Middle Ages, the square served as a site for markets, executions, knight tournaments, and festive receptions for visiting emperors.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: In 1638, Elector Maximilian I had the Mariensäule (Marian column) erected in the square to celebrate the end of Swedish occupation during the Thirty Years' War.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The construction of the Mariensäule was seen as an affront by the citizens, as it violated the 1315 privilege that reserved the square as city-owned territory.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: On October 9, 1854, the square was renamed Marienplatz (Mary's Square) to entrust the city to the Patrona Bavariae in hopes of saving it from a cholera epidemic.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: Between 1867 and 1909, the neogothic New Town Hall (Neues Rathaus) was built on the north side of the square by architect Georg von Hauberrisser.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The construction of the New Town Hall required the demolition of 21 traditional burgher houses and the old government building (Landschaftshäuser).
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The Old Town Hall (Altes Rathaus) stands on the east side of the square and is a reconstructed Gothic council hall.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The Glockenspiel in the tower of the New Town Hall was inspired by the medieval tournaments that used to be held in the square.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The buildings surrounding Marienplatz were severely damaged during the Second World War, resulting in the loss of historical buildings on the south side.
claims.subject: self
